title: A mechanism at several positions: what is the motion cycle?
summary: A linkage drawn in many positions at once. Faint ghosted copies show the sweep, one bold copy is the current position, a dotted curve is the path of a chosen point, and a star marks the instantaneous centre of the coupler.

media.alt: A four-bar linkage drawn many times in faint blue with one bold teal copy attached to ground points at x = 0 and x = 4, an amber dot on the coupler, a dotted closed path, a pink star far above marking the instant centre with dashed lines to it, and a grey ground bar.
media.caption: Reference render of class F4.2 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: What is the motion cycle?
read_the_figure.axes: x and y in metres on the plane, equal scale. Ground pivots at (0, 0) and (4, 0), with the ground bar drawn grey below. Teal: the current position (crank at 60 degrees). Faint blue: ghosted positions every 45 degrees of crank angle. Dotted: path of the amber coupler point. Pink star: instant centre I; dashed lines run from the crank and rocker tips to I.
look_at: Which link goes all the way round (the crank) and which only swings (the rocker)?
What is the shape of the dotted path of the coupler point, and how big is it?
Where is the instant centre and how is it found from the picture?
Which way is the amber coupler point moving right now?
as_drawn: Link lengths: crank 1.2, coupler 3.6, rocker 3.2, ground 4.0 (metres). Because 1.2 + 4.0 = 5.2 is less than 3.6 + 3.2 = 6.8, the shortest link can rotate fully: a crank-rocker.

At crank 60 degrees the instant centre is at (3.15, 5.46): the intersection of the lines through the two ground pivots and the crank and rocker tips. The coupler point's velocity is perpendicular to the line joining it to I.
Ghosts every 45 degrees overlap strongly and the 'I' label is clipped at the marker. Only one assembly configuration is shown; timing is not shown.
read_the_figure.proves: The geometry of the sweep, the closed path of the coupler point and where the instant centre is at one position. It does not show timing, speed or forces.
if_wrong: No ghosted positions: the range of motion is invisible.
No ground drawn: it is unclear which pivots are fixed.
An instant centre drawn without the lines that define it: it cannot be checked.

terms.meaning: Four rigid links joined by four pin joints, one link (ground) fixed.
The rotating input link, the floating middle link, and the oscillating output link.
If the shortest plus the longest link is less than the sum of the other two, the shortest link can rotate fully.
The path traced by a point attached to the coupler.
The point about which a moving link is turning at this instant; its velocity is zero.
The number of independent inputs needed to fix the position: 1 for a four-bar.

remember: Mobility in the plane: M = 3(n - 1) - 2 j for pin joints.
Instant centre of the coupler = intersection of the lines through the crank and rocker.
Velocity of a point = omega times its distance from I, perpendicular to the line to I.
Ghost the sweep; draw the ground; mark the special point.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Lines are links, circles are joints. Bold teal shows now, thin blue shows the past and the future of the motion. A dotted line is the trail of one point, an amber dot is that point at this instant, and a pink star with dashed lines is the instant centre construction.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A mechanism's motion is a family of poses. Drawing several at once turns an animation into one static picture where the range, the closed path and the crank-rocker character can be seen. The instant centre gives a single point about which everything on the coupler is turning right now, which makes velocities easy to read.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Ghosts at a fixed angle step hide timing: the path looks the same whether it is traversed fast or slowly. Too many ghosts turn the picture into a mesh. A mechanism has two ways to assemble (elbow up or down) and the picture shows one. And an instant centre far away, as here, is nearly a translation: it is easy to misplace.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: Ghosted positions show the range, which a single position cannot. The instant centre shows the construction rather than a number, so a reader can check it. Without both the figure is just a drawing of a linkage.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: To show timing mark the coupler curve at equal crank-angle steps. For performance, plot the transmission angle or the output angle against the input angle. For velocity use a velocity polygon. For several mechanisms, animate. For a given path, synthesise the linkage numerically.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Mark the coupler path with a dot at every 15 degrees of crank angle; add a second panel plotting the rocker angle against the crank angle.

steps.title: Mobility and the Grashof test
steps.note: Four links and four pins give one degree of freedom: one input drives everything. The Grashof inequality holds, so the 1.2 link makes full turns and the 3.2 link swings (between about 97 and 143 degrees).

steps.title: Velocity from the instant centre
steps.note: Checked numerically for a crank at 1 rad/s: the coupler turns at -0.235 rad/s (clockwise), |PI| = 3.26, so |v_P| = 0.768 m/s, and v_P dot (P - I) is zero to 2e-6.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) which link is the crank? (2) Where is the instant centre and what lines define it? (3) How far does the dotted path extend?

solution.text: The 1.2 m link on the left pivot (0, 0): it is the shortest and the Grashof test s + l < p + q passes, so it can rotate fully.
At (3.15, 5.46): where the line through the left pivot and the crank tip meets the line through the right pivot and the rocker tip (the two dashed lines).
The dotted curve extends from about x = -0.1 to 1.9 and y = 0.6 to 2.6: a closed loop, smaller than the ground length of 4.

worked.answer: Crank = the 1.2 m link; I at (3.15, 5.46) from the two dashed lines; a closed coupler loop about 2 m by 2 m.

analyze.q: The instant centre is far above the mechanism. What does that say about the motion of the coupler at this instant?
analyze.hint: A far centre means almost pure translation.

analyze.q: If the crank were lengthened to 2.6 m, would the linkage still be a crank-rocker?
What information does the figure lack that a timing study needs?

evaluate.q: A designer says 'the coupler point path is a nice egg, so the mechanism works'. What else do you need to check?
evaluate.hint: Transmission angle, timing, and the second assembly mode.

create: Plot the rocker angle against the crank angle for a full turn and mark the extreme positions.
Mark the coupler path with dots at equal crank-angle steps.

checks.q: How many degrees of freedom does a planar four-bar have?
Links 1.0, 2.0, 2.5 and 3.0. Is there a link that can rotate fully?
checks.hint: Shortest plus longest versus the other two.
checks.answer: 1.0 + 3.0 = 4.0 < 2.0 + 2.5 = 4.5: yes, the shortest link can rotate fully.

checks.q: The instant centre of the coupler is found at the intersection of two lines. Which two?
checks.hint: The lines along the links attached to ground.
checks.answer: The line through the left ground pivot and the crank tip, and the line through the right ground pivot and the rocker tip (where the two are not parallel).
